name: Iron Oxide Red (CI 77491)
regulatory: FDA 21 CFR 73.2250 (color additive); EU Cosmetic Reg. Annex IV; not a UV filter under FDA monograph but co-formulated with mineral UV filters as colorant for tinted (mineral / camouflage) sunscreens
metric: E(1%, 1cm) -- effective mass attenuation (absorption + Mie scattering) for pigment-grade ~300 nm primary particles dispersed in cosmetic film. Derived from k(L/g/cm) via E1% = 10 x k.
primary_sources: Marusak, Messier, White 1980 J Phys Chem Solids 41:981 -- canonical hematite alpha(lambda), single crystal: alpha = 11,560-44,840 cm-1 across NIR-UV. Conversion to E1% via E1% = alpha / (rho x ln10) approx alpha/1210 -> intrinsic crystal E1% = 10-37 across spectrum.

Sherman & Waite 1985 Am Mineral 70:1262 -- ligand-field band assignments for Fe3+: 6A1->4T1 ~880 nm, 6A1->4T2 ~650 nm, 6A1->4E,4A1 ~530 nm, plus pair-excitation ~485 nm and ligand-to-metal CT < 400 nm.

Morris et al. 1985 J Geophys Res 90:3126 -- submicron hematite powder diffuse-reflectance: pigments ~2x effective mass attenuation vs single crystal due to multiple-scattering path-length enhancement.
Castanedo-Cazares et al. 2014 Photodermatol Photoimmunol Photomed -- iron-oxide tinted SPF reduces VL transmittance + outperforms UV-only sunscreen in melasma (clinical anchor).
Dumbuya et al. 2020 J Drugs Dermatol 19:712 -- VLPF 5.4-7.07 at 4.85% and 27.25% iron oxide loadings (nonlinear; saturation evident).
Ezekwe et al. 2024 PPP 40:e12937 -- 71.9-85.6% HEV (415-465 nm) attenuation across SPF 35/50 tinted formulations.
Querry 1985 (refractiveindex.info) -- hematite n,k 0.21-55.6 um single-crystal optical constants.
physical_notes: Hematite is a pigment (200-500 nm primary), not a nano-UV-filter. Mie scattering at visible wavelengths is comparable to absorption -- the 'k' here is effective extinction (absorption + scattering) measured on dispersed dilute films.

Spectrum has a Tauc-like edge at 590 nm (2.1 eV bandgap, indirect) plus characteristic Fe3+ d-d shoulders at 530 nm (6A1->4E,4A1) and 650 nm (6A1->4T2). Strong CT absorption rises sharply below 500 nm into the UV.

Above the bandgap (lambda < 590 nm) extinction is dominated by interband absorption + scattering; below ~700 nm it tails off rapidly into the deep red/NIR where hematite is transparent (giving the red color).

In the UV (280-400 nm) hematite is a very strong absorber via O-2p -> Fe-3d charge-transfer, with k roughly comparable to or slightly above the visible peak. Adds material UVA1 protection (~340-400 nm) when used at >2-3% even though primary role is HEV blockade.

concentration_nonlinearity.model: f(c) = 1 - alpha * tanh(max(0, c - c0) / scale)
concentration_nonlinearity.rationale: Pigment-grade iron oxide saturates rapidly: Dumbuya 2020 shows VLPF 5.4 at 27.25% IO vs VLPF 7.07 at 4.85% IO (in fact LOWER at higher load due to film-density / thickness reduction), and Ezekwe 2024 shows 1-3% iron-oxide tints already block 72-86% HEV. Saturation kicks in by ~3% loading.
concentration_nonlinearity.source: Fitted to (a) Ezekwe 2024 71.9-86% HEV blockade at typical 1-3% iron oxide loads; (b) Dumbuya 2020 inverse-dose VLPF data; (c) Ruvolo 2018 PF-VIS 3.2-6.3 in iron-oxide-tinted formulations.

particle_size_correction.model: multiplier on E1%(lambda); pigment-grade is the cosmetic norm
particle_size_correction.source: Mie theory for hematite n~3.0+0.5i in visible. Optimum mass-specific extinction near 300 nm primary for HEV (lambda/~2 in pigment matrix). Smaller (<50 nm) ultrafine grades sacrifice scattering contribution; larger (>1 um) lose surface-area-to-mass advantage. Default = 300 nm reflects USP cosmetic-pigment spec.
particle_size_correction.note: Ultrafine iron oxides (~10-50 nm) used in transparent sunscreens have markedly lower visible-light attenuation per unit mass -- they are NOT a substitute for pigment-grade for HEV protection.

hev_model.absorbance: A(lambda) = E1%(lambda) x f(c) x g(d) x 100 x c_active_g_per_cm2
hev_model.note: 1.3 mg/cm2 = realistic facial sunscreen application (Ezekwe 2024); 2 mg/cm2 = ISO/FDA SPF reference.

validation.formulation: 1% IO Red, 1.3 mg/cm2 film (mono-pigment HEV test)
validation.source: Inferred from Ezekwe 2024 blended 1-2% load -> 72-86% (red contributes ~50% of effect)
Castanedo-Cazares 2014 / Ruvolo 2018 typical PF-VIS 3 at this loading
Dumbuya 2020 4.85% formula -> VLPF 7.07 = 86% blockade; rescaled for red-only fraction

validation.formulation: Tinted SPF 35 (red dominant, ~1.5% IO) -- Colorescience Total Eye 3-in-1
validation.source: Ezekwe 2024 -- discrepancy reflects synergy with TiO2/ZnO co-formulation; pure-IO model underestimates

validation.formulation: Castanedo 2014 melasma trial tinted UV-VL sunscreen
validation.source: Castanedo-Cazares 2014 Photodermatol Photoimmunol Photomed -- MASI improvement consistent with ~PF-VIS 2.5-3

validation_summary.note: Mono-pigment validation is within +/-5 pp; the Colorescience SPF 35 outlier reflects co-formulation synergy with TiO2/ZnO (the model is for iron-oxide-only contribution and underestimates the blended formulation).

caveats: Peak E1% = 75 is for pigment-grade ~300 nm hematite, well-dispersed in cosmetic film at <2% loading. Compare to OLD CHART value 2200 -- overstated by ~30x.
The red d-d shoulder near 530 nm and the 590 nm Tauc edge are characteristic and visible in real diffuse-reflectance pigment spectra (Morris 1985).
k below 280 nm and above 700 nm: hematite is a strong UV-C absorber but solar UV-C is filtered by atmosphere; >700 nm hematite is transparent (red color).
Effective k INCLUDES Mie scattering -- pigment particles of 200-500 nm in cosmetic film scatter visible light significantly. Don't double-count by adding a separate scattering term.
f(c) parameters (alpha=0.75, c0=0.5, scale=3) imply rapid saturation by 3% loading -- consistent with Dumbuya 2020 paradox (higher IO load -> LOWER VLPF) explained by film-density effect at 27% IO.
Co-formulated with TiO2, ZnO and (often) the other two iron oxides; full HEV blockade in real product is sum of all chromophores. This file gives the Red contribution alone.
